subject: ba
title: Economies of Scale, Economic Systems and Market Structures
objectives: Define and measure the size and scale of a business operation.
Distinguish between internal and external economies of scale.
Analyse economic systems: Capitalism, Socialism, and Mixed Economies.
Evaluate market structures: Perfect Competition, Monopoly, Monopolistic Competition, and Oligopoly.
study:
Economies of scale describe the cost advantage a firm gains as it increases its output — the core principle is that average cost per unit falls as the scale of production rises.

Key termInternal Economies of Scale — cost savings arising from the growth of the firm itself (technical, managerial, financial and marketing economies). External Economies of Scale — cost savings arising from the growth of the whole industry (a specialised labour pool, better shared infrastructure).

Managerial economies, specifically, come from a large firm being able to afford specialist managers rather than generalists doing everything. Financial economies let large firms borrow at lower interest rates. Push growth too far, though, and diseconomies of scale set in — the firm passes its optimum size and unit costs start rising again as it becomes harder to coordinate and manage. Business size itself isn't measured by one number but a combination of turnover (total sales revenue), market share, number of employees, and capital employed.

Economic systems set the rules for who owns production and how resources get allocated. Capitalism rests on private ownership and the price mechanism, driven by the profit motive — Classical Capitalism (Adam Smith) assumes near-perfect competition with a minimal state role, while Monopoly Capitalism reflects today's reality of imperfect competition and greater state intervention. Socialism puts the means of production under state or collective ownership, aiming at social welfare over private profit. A Mixed Economy blends both — markets do most of the work, but government regulates and directly participates in strategic sectors. Nigeria's economy is a mixed economy.

Exam tipDon't confuse economic systems (who owns production, economy-wide) with market structures (how competitive one particular market is) — they're tested as separate concepts even though both appear in this chapter.

Four market structures matter most. Perfect competition has many small firms, a homogeneous (identical) product, perfect information, and free entry/exit — each firm is a "price taker" with no power to influence the market price. Monopoly sits at the other extreme: a single seller, significant barriers to entry, and the power to be a "price maker." Monopolistic competition has many sellers offering differentiated products (different branding on essentially similar goods) — a blend of competition and monopoly. Oligopoly is dominated by a few large, interdependent firms — each must consider how rivals will react to its pricing, which sometimes leads to collusion through cartels (firms jointly fixing price/output) or price leadership (one firm sets price, others follow).
recap:
• Economies of scale: average cost per unit falls as output rises; internal (firm-specific) vs external (industry-wide).
  • Diseconomies of scale: past the optimum size, unit costs rise again.
  • Business size measured by: turnover, market share, employee count, capital employed.
  • Capitalism = private ownership + price mechanism; Socialism = state/collective ownership; Mixed economy = blend of both (Nigeria).
  • Market structures: Perfect Competition (many firms, homogeneous, price takers) · Monopoly (one seller, price maker) · Monopolistic Competition (many sellers, differentiated products) · Oligopoly (few interdependent firms, risk of collusion).
